clinicalPearls: Anterior knee pain localised to either side of the patellar tendon, characteristically aggravated by hyperextension and prolonged standing.
The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is one of the most richly innervated and vascularised intracapsular structures of the knee, so oedema or impingement is disproportionately painful.
Acute Hoffa's disease follows direct trauma or forced hyperextension; the chronic form relates to repetitive extension, patellar maltracking or genu recurvatum.
Hoffa's test reproduces pain on pressing the fat pad either side of the tendon as the knee is passively extended from flexion.
MRI on fluid-sensitive sequences shows fat pad oedema and may demonstrate superolateral impingement between the patellar tendon and lateral trochlea.
Frequently associated with patella alta, patellar maltracking or iatrogenic scarring from previous arthroscopy portals.
First-line management is conservative: activity modification, taping to unload the fat pad, and physiotherapy addressing quadriceps control and tracking.
Refractory cases may respond to a carefully placed corticosteroid infiltration or arthroscopic resection of hypertrophied/impinging tissue.
reference.pathophysiology: The infrapatellar fat pad is an intracapsular, extrasynovial structure lying deep to the patellar tendon; it is highly vascularised and densely innervated by branches of the femoral, common peroneal and saphenous nerves, making it a potent source of anterior knee pain. Acute trauma or repetitive forced hyperextension provokes haemorrhage and oedema, followed by inflammation, fibrosis and hypertrophy. The enlarged fat pad becomes impinged between the femoral trochlea and the tibia or patellar tendon during terminal extension, and longstanding cases may undergo metaplastic calcification or ossification. Predisposing factors include patella alta, patellar maltracking, genu recurvatum and iatrogenic scarring following arthroscopy.
additionalDifferentials: Chondromalacia patellae and patellofemoral pain syndrome
Osgood-Schlatter or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease in adolescents
Localised pigmented villonodular synovitis or intra-articular tumour
additionalInvestigations: MRI with fluid-sensitive sequences demonstrating fat pad oedema and impingement
Lateral radiograph to assess patella alta and any fat pad calcification or ossification
Skyline/Merchant views to evaluate patellar tracking and tilt
Dynamic ultrasound of the anterior knee
Diagnostic local anaesthetic infiltration of the fat pad
Standing alignment views to assess genu recurvatum
Arthroscopy for direct visualisation in refractory cases
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging anterior knee mass suggesting neoplasm rather than benign fat pad hypertrophy
Systemic features such as fever, night sweats or weight loss suggesting infection or malignancy
True mechanical locking or giving way pointing to meniscal or ligamentous pathology
Effusion with warmth and erythema suggesting septic arthritis or inflammatory arthropathy
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve with conservative measures that address patellar tracking and loading. Arthroscopic resection gives good outcomes in refractory impingement, although recurrent scarring can prolong recovery.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the problem as patellar tendinopathy and prescribing tendon loading, which aggravates impingement.
Overlooking underlying patella alta or maltracking that perpetuates symptoms.
Poorly placed corticosteroid injection risking fat pad atrophy or tendon weakening.
Treating incidental MRI fat pad oedema as clinically significant, or dismissing genuinely symptomatic changes.
Forgetting iatrogenic causes related to previous arthroscopy portals.
references: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
management: Modify activity and load, avoiding provocative knee hyperextension and prolonged standing
Undertake physiotherapy to correct patellar tracking with quadriceps and vastus medialis strengthening, and use patellar taping to offload and de-tilt the patella
Give anti-inflammatory analgesia and consider a corticosteroid infiltration of the fat pad for persistent pain
Address predisposing factors such as patella alta, patellar maltracking or genu recurvatum
Offer arthroscopic resection or debridement of the infrapatellar fat pad for impingement refractory to conservative care
Refer to orthopaedics and sports medicine when symptoms are refractory or recurrent
